measurement.weight.attribute.root_reason: Felt heaviness of held objects, contrasted with size, needs no earlier skill in the map; the learner only needs to hold objects and sense how heavy each is.

edges.why: Length and height are two of the separate attributes the statement says one object has, each with its own words.
Weight is the third named attribute, and it must be seen as a different attribute from length or size.
The statement starts after two objects have been compared directly by length or height, and the words report that result.
Choosing longer, shorter or taller over a general word like bigger requires seeing length or height as its own attribute.
The statement starts after two objects have been compared directly by weight, and heavier or lighter reports that result.
Choosing heavier or lighter over a general word like bigger requires seeing weight as an attribute separate from size.
Placing the marked string along the second object with one end lined up is a direct length comparison of string and object.
A tool suits a length when its marked units can span the object, which is the idea of laying units end to end.
The statement says the number at a mark counts whole units spanning from 0, which is length as the count of units.
A ruler is a number line whose numbers are lengths from 0, so a mark's number counts units from 0.
The crayon problem asks for the length between the 2 mark and the 7 mark, which is a difference within 10.
Lining up the 0 mark with one end and reading the far mark as the count of units depends on the numbers counting from 0.
Measuring the same length in two different units means laying each unit end to end and counting how many fit.
The reason a larger unit gives a smaller number is that fewer larger units span the same length.
The statement says the measurement in the larger unit is the smaller number, so the two numbers must be compared.
The table problem needs to know a foot is a longer unit than an inch to decide without measuring.
The inch, foot, centimeter and meter are the standard units met on a ruler, and each benchmark is matched to its marked length.
The first step is to recall a benchmark of about the size of the named unit.
Picturing copies of the benchmark laid end to end along the object is mental iteration of a length unit.
Both objects are measured in the same standard unit with a ruler before their lengths are compared.
How much longer one object is than another is a compare situation whose answer is the difference.
Finding the difference of the two measured lengths is a subtraction, and any method will do.
One length taped on to the end of another is an add-to situation with the result unknown.
Lengths that are combined into one whole length form a put-together situation with the total unknown.
The unknown length is a sum of two lengths within 100, and any method for the sum will do.
Lengths given in centimeters or inches are measurements in standard units, and the answer is stated with the unit.
A piece cut off a board is a take-from situation in which the length that is left is unknown.
Comparing two lengths to find how much longer one is is a compare situation with the difference unknown.
The unknown length is a difference of two lengths within 100, and any method for the difference will do.
Lengths given in inches or centimeters are measurements in standard units, and the answer is stated with the unit.
The hour is named by reading the numeral on the clock face that the hour hand points to.
Telling which number the hour hand has passed and what the long hand at 12 meant comes from reading whole hours.
Half past rests on the minute hand having gone halfway, or one of two equal shares, around the clock.
The hour and the two-digit minutes on a digital display are written numerals, such as 4 and 35, that must be read.
The hour is the number the hour hand has most recently passed, the same rule used when the hour hand sits between numbers.
Counting by fives from 12 around to the number nearest the minute hand gives the minutes past the hour.
Drawing the hands for h o'clock reverses reading it, with the minute hand at 12 and the hour hand at h.
The hands for half past h reverse reading it, with the minute hand at 6 and the hour hand halfway to the next number.
Placing the hour hand at h and the minute hand on a numbered position is the drawing skill extended here.
Counting by fives from 12 until reaching mm locates the number where the minute hand is drawn.
Placing the hour hand partway between h and the next number extends the halfway placement used for half past.
The drawn hands must match how minute and hour hands are read to the nearest five minutes.
The test problem gives the time as 7:20, which must be read as hour and minutes before drawing.
Writing h:mm uses the same layout read on a digital clock, with the hour before the colon and minutes after.
The hour and the minutes, spoken as number words, must be written as numerals, such as twenty-five as 25.
The statement says each clock reading such as 8:00 happens twice a day, so the reading itself must be understood.

money.coins.value.root_reason: Naming coins and recalling 1, 5, 10 and 25 cents is learned as a fact by association with the coins themselves, so no earlier skill in the map is required.

edges.why: Each count-on step uses the value of the coin kind being added, such as 25 for a quarter.
Nickels are counted on by 5s, which is the skip count by fives.
Dimes are counted on by 10s starting from the running total, such as 25 then 35 then 45.
Quarters are counted on by 25s, a skip count not found elsewhere in the map.
Pennies are counted on by 1s starting from the running total, which is counting forward from a given number.
The total value is the whole made by combining the values of the separate coins.
The cents sign names the unit in which coin values are stated, so a cent amount must be understood first.
The test problem asks to write the numerals 40 and 3 together with the money signs.
Amounts given as coins, such as 3 dimes and 2 nickels, are first turned into a value in cents.
Combining the amounts is a sum within 100 cents, and any method for the sum will do.
Money that is given to someone who already has some is an add-to situation with the result unknown.
Amounts of money that are combined into one total form a put-together situation with the total unknown.
The total is written with the correct sign, the cents sign or the dollar sign, as the statement requires.
Amounts given as coins, such as 3 quarters, are first turned into a value in cents.
Taking away or comparing amounts is a difference within 100 cents, and any method will do.
Spending money so that some is taken away is a take-from situation with the amount left unknown.
Comparing two amounts of money to find how much more one is is a compare situation with the difference unknown.
The unknown amount is written with the correct sign, the cents sign or the dollar sign.
Each category group is counted separately by counting its objects one at a time, up to 10.
The objects are already sorted into categories by an attribute, so what a category is must be understood.
The ordering is by the count of each category, which must first be found by counting each one.
Putting the categories from most to fewest requires comparing the numerals that give their counts within 10.
Each data point in the list is placed in the row of the category it belongs to.
One mark is drawn for each data point, which is recording how many with marks.
The chart also gives the count for each category, which is found by counting that row.
The count for each category is recorded as a numeral beside its row.
The number of data points in a category is found by counting its tallies or pictures one for one.
Each mark or picture stands for one data point, which is the marks-for-how-many idea.
The counts of the separate categories must be read from the chart before they are combined.
The total in all combines the counts of up to three categories, which is adding up to three numbers.
The counts of the two categories must be read from the chart before they are compared.
How many more or fewer is a compare situation whose answer is the difference of two counts.
The difference of the two category counts is a subtraction within 20, and any method will do.
Each category needs as many pictures as its count, so a set of a given number is drawn.
A picture graph is the form in which one picture stands for one data point in each category row.
The test data are given as numerals beside each pet, such as Cats 3, and must be read to know how many to draw.
A bar must end level with the scale number equal to the count, which is the same reading convention used to read bars.
The scale in ones from 0 works like a number line on which each number marks a length from 0.
The count is the number on a scale from 0 that is level with the bar's end, so whole numbers act as lengths from 0.
The learner reads the needed counts from the bar graph before combining them.
Asking for the combined count of categories is a put-together situation with the total unknown.
The combined count is a sum of two counts up to 10, and any method for the sum will do.
The known part is read from the bar graph before the unknown part is found.
A total with one part given and the other part unknown is a take-apart situation.
The unknown part is the total minus the known part, a subtraction within 20 in the test problem.
Both category counts are read from the bar graph before their difference is found.
How many more or fewer is a compare situation whose answer is the difference of two counts.
Both counts lie on a scale up to 10, so their difference is a subtraction within 10.
The data are whole-unit length measurements made with a ruler, and the plot's number line is labeled with that unit.
Finding the smallest and largest measurement requires comparing the measurement numbers.
The plot is drawn on a number line marked in whole units, with each X placed above its number.
